paragraphs.text: Donatists, why do you still let your bishops lead you astray? Their deceptive darkness has been scattered by clear light, their error has been exposed and their obstinacy overcome. Why do they still boast to you with empty lies? Why do you still believe men who have been defeated? When they tell you that the judge was bribed, what are they doing that is new? What else do all defeated men usually do when they refuse to agree with the truth, except lie about the judge's unfairness? Ask them, and let them first answer you this, if they can: why did they dare to come to Carthage and meet with us in one place for a conference? Some years ago we had already called on them publicly to meet, so that the truth might come out as we conferred and the dissension that divides us might be removed. But they fled from the truth itself and replied for the record: "It is unfitting that the sons of the martyrs and the offspring of traitors should come together in one place." Why, then, have they now been willing to meet with us? I suppose they would not have done what seemed unfitting to them unless they recognized that we are not the offspring of traitors. Or at least let them tell us why they said, "It is unfitting that the sons of the martyrs and the offspring of traitors should come together in one place," and afterwards came together with us in one place. What forced them to do what is unfitting? They were not brought in chains; they came entirely of their own free will. If they say, "Because the emperor had ordered it," then they do what is unfitting whenever the emperor orders it. Why, then, are they angry with some traitors or other who have nothing to do with our case? Handing over the Lord's books to persecutors is certainly unfitting, yet by this reasoning the traitor who did it bears no guilt, because the emperor had ordered it. We say this not according to the truth but according to their own perversity. For they themselves said it. The public records proclaim it: they said it in the official proceedings. It was not some unknown person who said this but their bishop of Carthage, Primian. Primian gave this in writing to the magistrate of Carthage and instructed his deacon to declare it for the record: "It is unfitting that the sons of the martyrs and the offspring of traitors should come together in one place." Well, we have come together in one place. What do they say to that? If they say, "It is not unfitting," why did they lie when they said it was unfitting? If they say, "It is unfitting," why did they do what is unfitting? There is only one way they could claim that they did not do what is unfitting and did not lie in those words of Primian. They would have to say: "It is indeed unfitting that the sons of the martyrs and the offspring of traitors should come together in one place, but we came together with you because we have recognized that you are not the offspring of traitors." If that is so, why did they throw those same slanders at us once they were meeting with us in one place? Was it perhaps so that we too should recognize that they are not sons of the martyrs? For "martyrs" means witnesses, and the witnesses of Christ are true witnesses. But these men have been found to be false witnesses. They charged others with the crime of betrayal, crimes that belonged to other people, and they could not prove even these.

Why do you still pay attention to human lies and not to divine testimonies? Why do you still believe men who have been defeated, and not believe the truth, which has never been defeated? For God's truth has borne witness to his Church through many proofs from the holy Scriptures, in the writings of the prophets and the Gospels, as we demonstrated in the conference itself. Scripture marked out the place where the Church of Christ was to begin, and the ends of the earth as the limit to which it was to reach. The Lord says that his Church will exist among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. The divine reading is recited that tells how it began from Jerusalem, where the Holy Spirit was first sent from heaven upon the gathered believers. The divine readings are recited that tell how it spread out from Jerusalem through places near and far. The names of the places are set out, and the names of the cities are made known, in which the Church of Christ was founded by the labour of the apostles. These places and cities were also found worthy to receive letters from the apostles. Your bishops themselves read those letters in your congregations, and yet they are not in communion with the churches of the places and cities that were found worthy to receive them. They charge those churches with some crimes or other committed by Africans, saying that these churches have perished through contact with them. Yet in this very conference that we recently held at Carthage, they themselves said that neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person.

They said this when we told them: "The council that you cite against Caecilian does no harm to Caecilian, who was absent, just as the council held in the matter of Maximian, at which Primian was condemned, does no harm to Primian, who was absent." For they produced a council at which seventy-odd bishops had condemned Caecilian in his absence, while about a hundred bishops of their own party are on record as having condemned Primian in his absence. So when we told them that the one council does no harm to Caecilian, just as the other does no harm to Primian, since both councils were held against absent men, they immediately found nothing to answer. In their dreadful predicament they said that neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person. This is what the Catholic Church always has on its lips against all human slanders, and now it can say it far more forcefully and far more freely, since what the truth has always held has been confirmed even by the admission of its enemies. Who, then, can bear this without deep sorrow? Who can hold back a groan? Who, considering it as it deserves, would not burst into tears and cries of grief? See: so that Primian, condemned by the bishops of Donatus's party, should not lose his bishopric, or so that the condemned Primian should not trouble Donatus's party, neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person. But so that Caecilian, whom his enemies likewise condemned in his absence, should not be considered a bishop, and should contaminate all the Christian nations to the ends of the earth, one case does prejudice another case and one person another person.

Suppose the churches of Pontus, Bithynia, Asia, Cappadocia and the other eastern regions, to which the blessed apostle Peter writes, were to cry out with the voice of unity itself: "Party of Donatus, we do not know what you are talking about. Why are you not in communion with us? If Caecilian did something wrong, which has not been proved or demonstrated to us, but even if he did something wrong, why does that prejudice us? If you will not listen to us, listen to yourselves saying: neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person. Or can your perversity go so far that these words hold good to keep Primian from prejudicing you, but do not hold good to keep Caecilian from prejudicing us?" Let the seven eastern churches to which the apostle John writes cry out in the same way, those of Ephesus, Smyrna, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea and Pergamum, and let them say: "What have we done to you, brothers, that you chose to belong to the communion of Donatus rather than ours? If Caecilian sinned, though you could not demonstrate his crime either, since he too was condemned in his absence just like your Primian, still, whatever sort of man he was, what have we done to you? Why are you, Christians, unwilling to have peace with Christians? Why do you invalidate in us the sacraments we share? What have we done to you? Why does Primian's case not prejudice the party of Donatus, unless it is because what you said is true: neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person? Why, then, does Caecilian's case prejudice the inheritance of Christ, in which we were planted by the labour of the apostles? The apostle John writes to one of us that it has a few names in Sardis of those who have not soiled their garments. Yet the garments of those few were not defiled by those in that same church who were unclean, because what you said is true: neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person. How, then, can the case and person of Caecilian prejudice us? Or if it does not, why do you separate yourselves from us?" Let the churches to which the apostle Paul writes also speak: those of the Romans, the Corinthians, the Philippians, the Colossians and the Thessalonians (Galatia and Ephesus have already been mentioned above). Let these too say: "Brothers, you who still wish to belong to the party of Donatus, every day you read the letters sent to us. In those very letters the apostle greeted us in the name of peace, saying, 'Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.' Why did you learn about peace by reading our letters, and yet refuse to keep it with us? We are set in such distant lands across the sea, and you charge us with the African Caecilian. Surely what you said is true: neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person. What is this private and peculiar sanctification of yours, which allows the case of the African Primian not to prejudice the African party of Donatus, and the person of Felician of Musti not to prejudice the person of Primian of Carthage, while African prejudices are sent all the way to us, and Caecilian's case prejudices us?"

Let the Catholic Church established in Africa itself, joined in communion with all those churches through the peace and unity of Christ, also speak. Let it say: "Neither does Caecilian's case prejudice me, though a sentence was pronounced against him in his absence by seventy bishops, because it does not prejudice the Church spread throughout the whole world, in whose communion I remain; or else let Primian's case prejudice the party of Donatus, since his own colleagues likewise condemned him in his absence at a larger council. But if it does not prejudice them because neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person, then this justice must be kept all the more toward the catholic unity of Christ, if the party of Donatus demands that it be kept toward itself." This is what the Catholic Church established in Africa proclaims: "Party of Donatus, you spoke these words, you acknowledged these words as your own, you even signed these words: neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person. I recite the name of Caecilian among the spirits of those who have long been at rest. You still see Felician, who condemned Primian, and you still have him with you in the body. In Primian's case itself you condemned Felician, and afterwards you joined him, a bishop just as before, to Primian and to yourself. If the principle that neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person, is strong enough that communion with Felician, who lives among you today, does not prejudice you, how does the memory of Caecilian, who died long ago, prejudice me?"

What answer can they give to this, the men who still boast to you of empty things, and of lies that will harm their own salvation unless they correct themselves? Why do they still say that we corrupted the judge so that a verdict would be given in our favour? Did we also corrupt your most distinguished bishop and advocate, a man held in such esteem among you, so that he would say such things on our behalf? For this is what we were striving for with all our strength, this is what we were pressing for: to show that the case and person of Caecilian, whatever sort of man he was, have nothing to do with the case and person of the Church, which God has strengthened with his holy testimonies. We pressed this point with the parables of the Gospel as well. The case and person of the weeds do not prejudice the case and person of the wheat, even though they grow together in the same field under the same rain until the harvest, when they must be separated. The case and person of the chaff do not prejudice the case and person of the grain, even though they are threshed together on the same threshing floor until they are separated by the final winnowing. The case and person of the goats do not prejudice the case and person of the sheep, even though both flocks are kept mingled in common pastures until the chief Shepherd separates them at the Last Judgement, some to the left and others to the right. The case and person of the bad fish do not prejudice the case and person of the good fish, even though they are held in the same nets until they are separated on the far shore, that is, at the end of the sea, which signifies the end of the age. By these parables and figures it was foretold that the Church would have good and bad members together until the end of the age, in such a way that the bad cannot harm the good. This holds while the bad are either unknown, or tolerated for the sake of the peace and tranquillity of the Church, when it would not be right to expose or accuse them, or when they could not be shown to be bad to the other good members. But the vigilance that seeks correction is not to rest. It works by rebuking, demoting, excommunicating and the other lawful and permitted forms of discipline that take place in the Church every day without harm to the peace of unity. This is done with charity preserved, in keeping with the apostle's command: "If anyone does not obey our word in this letter, take note of him and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed. Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but rebuke him as a brother." In this way discipline preserves patience and patience tempers discipline, and both are directed toward charity, so that neither patience without discipline fosters wickedness, nor discipline without patience destroys unity.

When the good do these things, they are not defiled by the bad. They do not share in their sins by consenting to them, and they depart from them, if not by bodily separation, then by the unlikeness of their spiritual life and the difference of their conduct. In this way they obey the Lord's command that says, "Depart from there, and touch nothing unclean." Those who think this is not to be observed spiritually fall, through vain arrogance, into what the Lord condemns through the same prophet when he says: "Those who say, 'Do not touch me, for I am clean,' are smoke in my anger." Your bishops thought they should do just this when the judge offered seats to both sides and they refused to sit with us. They said it was written that they should not sit with such people, understanding carnally rather than spiritually what is set down in the psalm: "And I will not sit with the ungodly." Yet they did something that is equally forbidden in the very same passage of the psalm, where the prophet says: "And I will not go in with those who do wrong." So if they refused to sit with us because they knew us to be wicked, or thought us so, why did they go in with us, the holy on one side and the polluted on the other, when this is likewise forbidden? Is it not because by failing to understand the holy Scriptures and by thinking carnally they have destroyed unity itself?

So the bad do not defile the good when they are placed in the same field, on the same threshing floor, in the same pastures, in the same nets. The good are not in communion with them but with God's altar and sacraments. Those who consent to the deeds of the bad are the ones in communion with the bad, for it is written: "Not only those who do these things, but also those who approve of those who do them."

When the bad are tolerated because peace must be preserved, they are not being sought out as partners in shared wickedness. The wheat drinks the sweet rain together with the weeds, yet keeps its fruitfulness and is not turned into the barrenness of the weeds; rather, both grow together until the harvest, lest when the weeds are gathered the wheat be uprooted with them. In that case the bad have no participation with the good in salvation or in perdition, for "what participation has righteousness with wickedness?" The bad have no fellowship with the good in the kingdom or in the eternal fire, for "what fellowship has light with darkness?" The bad have no harmony with the good in life and will, for "what harmony has Christ with Belial?" The good have no share with the bad, either in the punishment of crime or in the reward of devotion, for "what share has a believer with an unbeliever?" Within the same nets, until they reach the shore, they receive the divine sacraments alike. Yet the good are in fellowship and the bad are not; the good are in harmony and the bad are out of tune; the good have their share in mercy, the bad in judgement. For the Church sings to the Lord of mercy and judgement, and "whoever eats unworthily eats judgement" not on another but "on himself." Indeed, both Judas and Peter received their share of the same bread from the same hand of the Lord. And yet what fellowship, what harmony, what share did Peter have with Judas, since neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person?

There are bad people who go out, of whom it is written, "They went out from us, but they were not of us." There are also bad people who seem to be inside, of whom the blessed Cyprian speaks very plainly when he says: "For even if there seem to be weeds in the Church, neither our faith nor our charity ought to be hindered, so that because we see weeds in the Church we ourselves withdraw from the Church." Your bishops dared not answer these words at all, though they argued at length and in vain that the weeds in the parable were not foretold as being in the Church, because the Lord said, "The field is this world," and did not say, "The field is the Church." We, however, said that "world" was used to signify the Church, as Cyprian also understood it, because the Church was foreshadowed as one that would exist throughout the whole world. To this they replied that "world" is always used in a bad sense, and cited testimonies from Scripture, since it is written, "If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him," and other such passages. We answered that in Scripture "world" is used not only in a bad sense but also in a good one, and among other passages we cited the one where it is written: "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself." Surely he reconciles to himself nothing but the Church. So whether the bad go out, or whether they are inside, either unknown or recognized, the mercy and justice of God bring it about that the bad do no harm to the good, provided the good do not consent to their evil deeds. Each bears his own burden, and the son does not take on the sins of the father unless he has imitated him in evil, but "the soul that sins shall itself die."

So when anyone consents to evil with the bad, he now has one case with them and becomes one person with the whole fellowship of the bad. Therefore, when they perish together and are condemned together, it is each one's own case and own person that prejudices him, not another's. But when good and bad together hear the same word of God and together receive the sacraments of God, and yet the causes of their actions differ and they act as different persons because their wills differ, some eating the same holy food worthily and others unworthily, then neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person.

And so, whatever testimonies of the divine scriptures your bishops were able to cite, in which the church was foretold as pure of all admixture of wicked people, those testimonies foretold the church not as it is now but as it will be after this mortal life, in life eternal. And whatever testimonies of scripture they put forward about sons, whom they wanted to share one cause with their parents because of what the parents deserved, not because they imitated their wickedness: not understanding them, they forced the divine testimonies to fight against one another. They did not bring both of God's sayings into harmony by distinguishing different times, causes and persons. Just as they themselves were fighting against us, they wanted the divine teachings to fight among themselves. No wonder they did not understand the peace of God's scripture, when they did not have peace with his church.

We, however, accepted both sets of testimonies and showed that they agree. For we accepted the text they cited in their letter as spoken to the church, "The uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you," and also the text that is written, "Let both grow until the harvest." But we said that the second applies in the field, while the first will apply in the barn. Indeed, they themselves had long argued that the tares, which were allowed to grow together with the wheat until the harvest, are not in the church but in the world. In this they went against the understanding of the martyr Cyprian, who said: "Even if there seem to be tares in the church, our faith or our charity ought not to be hindered, so that because we see tares in the church we ourselves withdraw from the church." They also refused to agree that the church can be signified by the name "world," against the words of the apostle, who said, "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself," and against the words of the Lord himself, who said, "The Son of Man came not to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him." For the world cannot be reconciled to God and saved through him unless "world" is understood to mean the church, which alone is reconciled to God through him and saved. Yet even these men were defeated by the evidence of the truth in the likeness we cited from the gospel. There both good and bad fish are held mixed together within the same nets until they are separated on the shore, that is, at the end of the age. So they confessed that the wicked are mixed in the church until the end of the age. But they said that these are hidden, because they are unknown to the priests in the same way that fish within the nets are not seen by the fishermen while they are still in the sea. How then can the prophetic testimony they set down in their response, in which it was said to the church, "The uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you," be understood to apply to this time, when the church is compared to nets? For they confessed that while those nets are still in the sea, bad fish are mixed with the good, even if hidden. Hence it is plain that only in the age to come, after the judgment, will no uncircumcised or unclean person pass through the church. O the force of truth, which tortures its enemies not in the flesh but in the heart, so that they confess it against their will!

See, what we were saying has been made plain. The times of the church must be distinguished. She is not now what she will be after the resurrection. Now she has the wicked mixed in with her; then she will have none at all. The divine testimonies in which God foretold that she would be utterly free from all admixture of the wicked refer to that future purity of hers, not to the mixture of this present time. See, even these men, who said that hidden wicked people are now mixed in with her, were compelled by the truth of the gospel to confess exactly this. See, the unclean person now passes through her, even if hidden. So this is not the time foretold when the prophet says, "The uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you." Now, then, they do pass through, even if hidden. Indeed, the very words "no longer" show that they used to pass through before but will not pass through any more. They also demanded of us, to stir up ill will, how the devil could have sown tares in the church of Christ. Yet they themselves admitted that the wicked are mixed into the church, hidden ones at least, and they would not consider that these were certainly sown by the devil.

Even the point they thought they had cleverly discovered they turned against themselves instead. Suppose the Lord compared the church to nets that gather good and bad fish alike because he wanted the wicked in the church to be understood as lurking rather than manifest, unknown to priests just as fishermen do not know what their nets have caught beneath the waves. Then by the same reasoning the church was also compared to a threshing floor in order to foretell that manifest wicked people too would be mixed with the good in it. For the chaff that is mixed with the grain on the threshing floor does not also lie hidden under the waves. It is so plain to everyone's eyes that it is rather the grain that is hidden within it, while the chaff is in full view. We had cited this likeness of the threshing floor too from the gospel, among the others, and they could write nothing against it in their letter except that the prophet Jeremiah said, "What has chaff to do with wheat?" He said this because they are not alike, not because they cannot be mixed; because they will not be together in the barn, not because they are not threshed together on the floor. Besides, when Jeremiah said this he was not speaking about the people of God but about the dreams of men and the visions of prophets, since these two cannot be compared by any likeness, just as the emptiness of chaff cannot be compared to the fullness of wheat.

Your bishops did try to deny that the gospel says the church is compared to a threshing floor. But they were soon refuted when the words of the gospel were cited, and so they turned to claiming that there too the wicked meant are hidden, not manifest. Of these it is written: "He will come bearing his winnowing fork in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor; he will store the grain in the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire." So judge for yourselves: open your eyes, turn your ears to the truth. They themselves said that the Lord compared the church to nets because he wanted the wicked in it to be understood as lurking rather than manifest, so that priests do not see them, just as fishermen do not see the fish within the nets beneath the waves. If so, is a threshing floor also threshed under water or under the earth? Is the grain trodden out at night rather than in the sun? Does a blind farmer work it? How much better it would be for them to correct themselves than to pervert the holy gospels and try to twist the Lord's words to fit the empty error of their own minds! Either the Lord gave that likeness of the fish too not because the wicked in the church are hidden but only because they are mixed in, or else each case was given its own likeness: the fish because of the hidden wicked, the threshing floor because of the manifest wicked. Just as the fish are mixed until the shore, so the chaff is mixed with the good in the church until the winnowing fork. Indeed, these men themselves prompt us to understand the chaff on the threshing floor as the manifest wicked in the church, since they want the rejected fish within the nets in the water to be understood as the hidden wicked, because priests do not know the wicked any more than fishermen know those fish. For why should we not say, "So, then, the chaff stands for the manifest wicked, because the threshers see it in the open"? But just as the fish cannot be separated before they come out onto the shore, so the chaff cannot be winnowed out before the appointed end. Meanwhile God guards the innocence of his saints and faithful, like that of the good fish and the plump grain, so that within these nets the kinds mixed in with them, which are to be rejected, do not harm them, and on this threshing floor the chaff mixed in with them, which is to be winnowed out, does not harm them. For, as they themselves said, reread and signed, neither can one case prejudice another case nor one person prejudice another person.

Perhaps they would deny that they said these words, if they could not be convicted by their own signatures. See how carefully matters were arranged for your salvation, so that we each signed our own words. They were utterly unwilling for this to be done, and in the end were driven to do it by shame. For their words survive in which they refused to do it, and again other words in which they agreed to do what they had at first refused. Everything was written down; everything was signed. The reason they seemed unwilling to sign was so that they could deny having said what they had said and bring false charges against the judge about falsified records. Since they cannot do that now, they say that the judge himself was corrupt. Yet no one but they themselves made him judge against them, since they said so much against themselves and in our favor, and they signed their own statements, even if under compulsion and unwillingly, so that they could not deny them. That, then, is why they did not want to sign: so that they would be free to deny what they had said by falsely alleging that the records had been tampered with. And later, when the judge pressed them, they consented because they sensed that everyone could see that by refusing to sign they were showing nothing except that they were afraid to have their own words read back to them. They preferred to defend their statements later with whatever fog they could raise rather than condemn them so quickly.

But see, we beg you, how by their very defense they entangle themselves still worse, pleading our case and utterly destroying their own. For after the conference, when they had been defeated and wanted to appeal, these words were put to them, and when you ask them what they did, they try to defend those words by entangling themselves still worse. They think you so lacking in sense that you will not realize they have been beaten on every point, when they tell you things they would never say at all if they could find anything useful to say. Who could bear to hear defeated men complain that the sentence against them was pronounced at night? As if the need to hear a case did not often hold judges so that they are forced to sit far into the night! Or as if what is said were untrue just because it is said at night! They do not hear the scripture crying out, "By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he made it known," and again, "To proclaim your mercy in the morning, and your truth through the night." As for their saying that it was at night the persecutors came to seize the Lord, they do not notice that in those very hours of the night the Lord also preached the truth to his disciples. Nor were they willing to note what is written, that the apostle Paul prolonged his sermon until midnight. If they had anything true to say, the night could not have stopped them. But they were indeed suffering a very dark night in their minds when they brought forward so much against themselves and did not correct their perverse minds by the light of truth. And it was certainly still day when they raised a plea against us about the time limit, as is done in the law courts, saying that the case had lapsed and could no longer be heard at all. They did not understand that they had shown people nothing except how much they feared its being heard, since then their perversity and the catholic truth would be displayed.

It was still day when, wanting to overturn the judgment of Miltiades, bishop of Rome, by which Caecilian was cleared and acquitted, they said that Miltiades himself had been a traditor, one who handed over the scriptures. When they were required to prove this charge, they read out very lengthy records in which the name of Miltiades did not appear as having handed over anything. They also read other records, in which it was stated that Miltiades had sent deacons with letters from the emperor Maxentius and the praetorian prefect to the prefect of the city, so that they might recover the places that had been taken from the Christians during the persecution. When no crime whatever on the part of Miltiades appeared there either, they said that the earlier records of the handing-over had named a certain Strato as a traditor, because one of the deacons whom Miltiades sent to recover the places was also called Strato. They contended, without showing it, that this was the same man. They did not even show that the Strato who had handed over the scriptures had been a deacon. And even if he had been, we answered them that a short time before there had been two deacons named Peter among the clergy of the Roman church. Blind in mind as they were, they wove together dark slanders, and added a most obvious falsehood besides: that not only the name but also the places, districts and persons matched, showing that it was the same Strato and not another. In fact nothing at all in those records matched except the similarity of the name. Human custom is full of such cases, so that not only two but even more people are called by the same name. Indeed, they themselves loudly insisted that their own Donatus of Carthage must be distinguished from Donatus of Casae Nigrae, so that he, whom they hold in high esteem, would not be thought to have been condemned in the judgment of Miltiades, because, they said, it was not Donatus of Carthage who had been sent against Caecilian to the episcopal judgment of Miltiades. Such thick night did they carry in their hearts that they did not want Donatus disgraced by the likeness of his own name, yet wanted Miltiades stained by the likeness of someone else's. Now they are said to be adding the name Cassian to Strato as well, which they kept quiet about at the conference, as though Strato alone could have had a namesake and Cassian could not. Hindered by their inner night, they could not notice that there were not only two Johns, one the Baptist and the other the Evangelist, but also two Simons, one Peter and the other the magician; indeed, even within the very small number of the apostles, there were not only two Jameses, one the son of Alphaeus and the other the son of Zebedee, but also two Judases, one a saint and the other a devil. Anyone equally blind in mind who slandered the holy apostle Jude with the crime of Judas the traitor would be imitating none other than these men. So it is no wonder if, after so long a time, the reputation of Miltiades has to put up with slanderers like these concerning two Cassians or two Stratos, just as the truth of the gospel has to put up with such people concerning two Herods. Because it is not specified which Herod died soon after the infants were killed in Christ's stead and which Herod persecuted the Lord together with Pilate, they think there was only one and charge the gospel with falsehood, just as these men think there was only one Strato or one Cassian and charge Miltiades with the stain of handing over the scriptures. And yet those others err more excusably, because not only the name but also the rank matches, since each is called King Herod. These men, however, lied that the rank matched, for they could nowhere read that both had been deacons.

It was still day when they turned to the Council of Cirta, if indeed a gathering of barely eleven or twelve bishops should be called a council. From its records we had read out that some of those who, together with Secundus of Tigisis, pronounced sentence against Caecilian had been traditors. Wanting to show that these records were false, they said that in a time of persecution those eleven or twelve bishops could not have gathered in any house. To prove that it was a time of persecution, they produced acts of the martyrs, so that by examining the days and consuls it would be clear what time it was. They were shown to have produced these acts of the martyrs against themselves, for those acts made it plain that during that time of persecution Christian congregations regularly assembled. It was thus established that it was not incredible that those bishops too, as the records stated, had likewise met in a private house. Their purpose was to ordain a bishop in secret for a congregation that was able to assemble even in time of persecution, as the acts of the martyrs showed, and he himself could then also ordain clergy for himself in secret, in such great need, since the previous bishop and his clergy were shown to have lapsed by the letter of Secundus himself, which they had cited. Prompted by these acts of the martyrs that they themselves produced, we looked into other acts of martyrs as well. We found and reported that while the persecution was raging, a private house, which they had denied could happen, was granted for a gathering of Christians, and that martyrs were baptized in prison. This was so that they might see how far from incredible it was that a few bishops gathered in a private house in time of persecution, when the sacraments of Christ were celebrated even in the prison where men were held shut up for the faith of Christ. Who, then, does not see how much they helped you by producing the acts of the martyrs, unless he has in his heart a night like the one they had who did not see these things?

They also made false charges against the Cirta records themselves because days and consuls were given there, and they demanded that we produce some church councils in which days and consuls were recorded. They themselves produced a Council of Carthage held without day or consul. They also said that Cyprian's council did not have consuls, although the day is given there, whereas in their council of Carthage not even the day is given. We, for our part, showed that the Roman council of Miltiades, which we had at hand, had both the day and the consuls, just like the council of Cirta. For we did not then have time to search on the spot through the ancient church archives to show that this had been the custom of earlier generations too. Nor did we want to raise empty charges against them in turn, asking why a day was found in Cyprian's council but not in theirs, since they wanted to contrive pointless delays, which we were trying to avert. For they even demanded that we show from the holy scriptures some place where days and consuls were written down, as if councils of bishops had ever been put on a level with the canonical scriptures, or as if they themselves could produce from the holy scriptures a council where apostles sat as judges and either condemned or acquitted someone who had been accused. Nevertheless we answered that the prophets too committed their books to writing with the times noted at the start and precisely defined: in what year of which king, in what month of the year, on what day of the month the word of the Lord came to them. We did this to show how emptily and slanderously they were raising utterly pointless questions about the days and consuls of episcopal councils. For this variation can occur in manuscripts, since some copyists are more careful and also write out the days and consuls, while others leave them out as superfluous. So, for example, the manuscript from which we first read the judgment of Constantine, in which he declared between the parties that Caecilian was innocent and that they were utterly slanderous, did not have the day and consul, but another manuscript, which we later produced against their false charges, did. At that point too they had loudly protested, to stir up ill will, that we read the emperor's letter without day and consul. Yet they themselves read out other letters of the same emperor, in the case of Felix, who ordained Caecilian, without day and consul, letters which with astonishing blindness they produced against themselves. We raised no objection to them over this, so as not to fill the necessary time with superfluous words as they did. But we say these things now so that you at least may open your eyes and be free of the dark night that your bishops carried in their hearts. They objected that the judge's hearing ended in a sentence given at night, while they themselves, wrapped in inner darkness in broad daylight, said so much against themselves with astonishing blindness.

The records of proceedings before the magistrate of Carthage contain the express words of Primian, where he says that our forebears harassed their fathers with various exiles. At the conference they try to prove that Caecilian was condemned to exile by the emperor on the accusation of their forebears. In their letter they say that their communion is the church of truth, the church that suffers persecution, not the one that inflicts it. Yet they try to show that Caecilian was condemned by the emperor's judgment while their own forebears were prosecuting him, and they say that this was done not through Donatus of Casae but through the man they praise above all others, Donatus of Carthage. This is what they are now said to be boasting of in their writings, spread through their own people, in which, defeated, they accuse the judge because a truth delivered by night refuted the night of their hearts. That Donatus, that very Donatus, I say, whom they called the ornament of the church of Carthage and a man of a martyr's glory, they wished to commend by saying that at the hearing before the emperor Constantine he himself both charged Caecilian as a defendant and convicted him. So, then, that man of a martyr's glory charged and accused Caecilian at the emperor's hearing, and that hearing was followed by Caecilian's condemnation: at the accusation and urging of that man of a martyr's glory, Caecilian was condemned by the emperor. This we proved false. We read out the letter of that same emperor, produced from the public archive, in which he testifies that he heard and judged between the parties, and in which, having acquitted and cleared Caecilian, he expressed his abhorrence of their slanders. Against it they could find nothing whatever to answer, and they produced other documents which confirmed it, against themselves. It was therefore established that Caecilian was accused before the emperor by their forebears, but it was not established that he was condemned; on the contrary, it was established that he was acquitted. But even so, see for yourselves how much your bishops have helped our case by wishing to glory even in that falsehood. For if that Donatus, a man of a martyr's glory, charged Caecilian at the emperor's hearing, and if Caecilian was condemned by the emperor at the accusation and urging of that man of a martyr's glory, let them answer you: when these things were taking place, who was the martyr? Was it Donatus, who was prosecuting a man before the emperor, or Caecilian, who was being condemned by the emperor while Donatus prosecuted him? Where now is that defining rule of theirs, that the communion of Donatus is the church of truth, the one that suffers persecution, not the one that inflicts it? Look: Caecilian suffers it, Donatus inflicts it. Which of them is the man of a martyr's glory?

Pay attention, take note, and do not let yourselves be led any longer into a deadly error. God has deigned to disclose the truth that was hidden from you, and God has deigned to refute the falsehood that was spread over you like a fog. Why are you still ungrateful for so great a kindness? This, surely, is what they kept telling you; this is how their cunning deceit darkened the eyes of your hearts; and even now, convicted as they are, they boast of it and tear us to pieces with it: that we inflict persecution and they suffer it. This is all that is left to them, beaten on every side, with which to keep raising mists before the uninstructed: on this ground they present themselves as the church of truth, because it suffers persecution and does not inflict it. So do not let them deceive you any longer. What we do to them is what they boast that their forebears, and the very man they extol as a man of a martyr's glory, did to Caecilian. He worked before the emperor to have Caecilian convicted and condemned by the emperor's judgment; we too have worked to have these men, once convicted, suffer similar things. If he did wrong, why was Donatus doing this to Caecilian? But if he did right, why should the Catholic Church not do this to the party of Donatus? In fact neither do they doubt that it is rightly done, since they boast that their forebears, whom they praise so highly, did it; nor do we doubt it, since we cannot deny that it must be done to them: namely, that the restless who are not corrected by words should be restrained, without shedding of blood, by some very mild penalty of the laws. And if the emperor, perhaps moved by the obstinacy of a sacrilegious mind, has decreed that it should be punished more severely, let the judges act more mildly, for they have always been permitted to soften and temper a sentence. Meanwhile, then, although it cannot be shown that Caecilian was condemned by the emperor Constantine, that error of yours has been removed by which you thought that the true church is the one that suffers persecution, not the one that inflicts it; for Donatus inflicted it and Caecilian suffered it. And if the party of Donatus suffers persecution, the party of Maximian suffers it along with them, and they themselves affirm that it is not the church of Christ. Hence inflicting persecution is no sign of wickedness, since the good inflict it on the wicked and the wicked on the good; and suffering persecution is no proof of righteousness, since not only the good suffer it for godliness, but the wicked also suffer it for wickedness.

It remains for you, then, now that error has been driven out, to see and hold fast to the church of Christ, the Catholic Church, but not to choose it on the ground that it suffers persecution. For when the Lord had said, "Blessed are those who suffer persecution," he added, so that heretics might not boast of it, "for righteousness' sake." You yourselves know what great evils the raving clergy and circumcellions of the party of Donatus have done to our people. Churches have been burned, the holy books thrown into the flames, private houses burned as well; people have been dragged from their homes, everything in them carried off or destroyed, and they themselves beaten, mangled and blinded. Nor could they keep from murder, although it is milder to take a man from this light by death than to take the light of his eyes from him while he lives. They went after people not to seize them and carry them off somewhere, but simply so that they should suffer these things. Yet we do not count our people righteous because they suffered these things, but because they suffered them for Christian truth, for the peace of Christ, for the unity of the church. But as for the other side, under so many and such severe laws, and under the great power the Lord has given the Catholic Church, what do they suffer that is anything like this? If they are ever punished with death, either they kill themselves, or they are killed while their bloody violence is being resisted; and that is not for belonging to the communion of the party of Donatus, nor for the error of a sacrilegious schism, but for their own blatant crimes and outrages, which they commit like bandits, with savage fury and cruelty. For the party of Donatus as such, they scarcely suffer anything like what they said Caecilian suffered at Donatus' urging.

Either, then, not all persecution is unjust, or it should not be called persecution when it is just. Therefore the party of Donatus either suffers a just persecution or suffers no persecution at all, because it suffers justly. Caecilian, however, did not suffer justly, since he was proved innocent and acquitted. They denied this, of course, and claimed instead that he was condemned by the emperor, and in doing so they admitted that their forebears, and above all Donatus, whom they praise so lavishly, persecuted Caecilian. But they could not prove in the least that he was convicted and condemned; on the contrary, by reading out many things against themselves they too confirmed what we were saying, that he was acquitted and cleared. And yet they boast that freedom of choice has been granted them by the emperor. Defeated and confounded, they were demanding even now to be granted what their forebears would not grant Caecilian, whom they accused before the emperor in this way, and whom these men even chose to claim, falsely, had been condemned by the emperor at their accusation. If free will must be granted to everyone, it should have been granted first to Caecilian; if these matters are not to be entrusted to a human judge but rather left to God, then Caecilian should never have been accused before the emperor in the first place.

Wake up at last! Do not let a hellish sleep hold you bound, do not let wicked habit sink you any further into the depths of sacrilegious error. Now be in harmony with peace, cleave to unity, yield to love, give way to truth. Recognize the Catholic Church, which began from Jerusalem and is spreading everywhere: the church with which the party of Donatus is not in communion, and which the case of Caecilian does not prejudge. For he was cleared so often, acquitted so often; yet even if he were not innocent, one case does not prejudice another, nor one person another. These words the whole church throughout the world proclaims, and its member in Africa also cries out: 'I know the testimony of God; I do not know the affair of Caecilian. I believe he was an innocent man hounded by your forebears, since I read that he was acquitted so many times. But whatever his case may be, it does not prejudice my case; whatever kind of person he may be, it does not prejudice my person. You said this yourselves, you put your signatures to it: one case does not prejudice another, nor one person another. See, the Lord says, "among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem." Let us hold the divine truth in the one church, and at last put an end to human quarrels.'

Were they able in any way, after the conference itself, to defend those words of theirs, in which they said that one case does not prejudice another nor one person another? Or did they not rather entangle themselves far more intricately? For in some of their writings they said this: "It has been recalled from memory that we said one case does not prejudice another and one person does not prejudice another, but this was said in its proper context: 'we are not prejudiced by those whom we have either rejected or condemned.' But as for those who descend from Caecilian's ordination, whom their origin counts as guilty through their predecessor, how could they not be bound by the crimes of their ordainer, when the rope of sins, stretched out through the succession, must make sharers in sin all whom it has bound with the bond of communion?" What an extraordinary defense! So thick and clinging is the mud in which their feet have stuck that, trying to pull them out, they plant their hands and their heads in it to no avail and, floundering in the same mud, are bound up in it more tightly. For among those whom they mention having either rejected or condemned, that is, among the Maximianists, they have Felician with them: the man who condemned Primian, and whom they condemned in Primian's cause. Why is it that they strive to entangle the Catholic Church of these times in a rope reaching so far, from Caecilian down to the present, and do not notice their own chain so close at hand? Splendid indeed is that sentence of Bagai about Maximian and his associates: "The chain of sacrilege," it says, "drags very many into partnership in crime." Felician, then, was being dragged by that chain. If Felician does not prejudice them, why does Caecilian prejudice us? Or perhaps one case prejudices another where they want it to, but not where they do not, and at their whim an ancient rope is stronger than a new chain? Maximian does not prejudice Felician, who was condemned through him; Maximian and Felician do not prejudice Primian, who was condemned by them; Maximian does not prejudice those who were granted a delay, with whom he was associated in one schism; Felician does not prejudice the party of Donatus, by which he was received back in the same rank, and the baptism he gave in sacrilegious schism was not undone there. And yet Caecilian prejudices so many Christian nations: he who was condemned once in his absence, as Primian was, and acquitted three times in his presence, as Primian was not! A man long dead and unknown prejudices us; yet a living man does not prejudice them, though we read that they condemned him a little while ago and we see that he is now associated with them. Caecilian's rope is wound around us, who do not even know him; but Felician's chain is not wound around them, though their own sentence against him is read out, in which that very chain is condemned. They may say, 'We received those whom we condemned, for the sake of the peace of Donatus, because one case does not prejudice another nor one person another'; and we may not say, 'Because of those whom you condemned we do not abandon the peace of Christ, because one case does not prejudice another nor one person another'! What brazen faces! What darkness of madness! They throw a verdict given by night in the judge's face, while in the night of their own hearts they grope, stumble and fall, quarrelling furiously against us and saying so much in our favor!

Besides this, they even now dare to cite testimonies from the prophets and apostles, which we answered comprehensively at that conference. We showed that the holy prophets themselves lived among the wicked in one temple, under the same priests, amid the same sacraments, and yet were not defiled by the wicked, because they knew how to distinguish between holy and unclean, not, as these men think, by physically dividing the people, but by judging well and living well. And they did this without ceasing, so that in that great house in which they were, where, as the apostle says, some vessels are for honor and some for dishonor, they cleansed themselves from such people by the difference in their way of life, and were vessels for honor, useful to the Lord, always ready for every good work. But it is a good thing that out of the many testimonies which they inserted, without understanding them, into the letter they produced and read out at the conference, they have now, defeated after the conference, cited a testimony from the prophet Haggai as if it were the chief one. For in this very prophet we can demonstrate far more clearly what we maintain: that it is not bodily but spiritual contact, which comes about through consent, that defiles people, since that consent makes their cause one.

For when the Lord willed to destroy the wicked even by a visible punishment, he himself separated the righteous from them by a warning: Noah and his household from those he was about to destroy by the flood; Lot from those he was about to consume with fire; his people from the congregation of Abiram, which he was soon to wipe out. So too the man who did not have a wedding garment was ordered to be bound and thrown out, not by those who had issued the invitations, but by the Lord himself, whose banquet it was. For that man was not like a fish under the waves, unable to be seen by the inviters as a fish cannot be seen by the fishermen. Accordingly, lest it be thought, as these men think, that he was just one man who had crept in secretly among the crowd without their knowledge, the Lord did not delay to indicate at once that in that very one, whom he ordered to be bound hand and foot and thrown out of the banquet into the outer darkness, we must understand a great company of the wicked, among whom the good, fewer in number, live at the Lord's banquet. For after saying, "Bind his hands and feet and throw him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth," he immediately added, "For many are called, but few are chosen." How is this true, when only one out of many had been thrown into the outer darkness, unless that one figured the great body of all the wicked who are mixed in at the Lord's banquet until the Lord's judgment? From these the good meanwhile separate themselves in heart and in conduct, eating and drinking the body and blood of the Lord together with them, but with a great distinction. The good, in honor of the Bridegroom, are clothed in the wedding garment, seeking not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ; the wicked do not have the wedding garment, that is, the most faithful love of the Bridegroom, and seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. And so, though at one and the same banquet, the good eat mercy and the wicked judgment; for the song of that banquet is the one I mentioned above: "Of mercy and judgment I will sing to you, O Lord."

Not that church discipline is asleep on that account and fails to rebuke the restless. For we do not separate from the people of God those whom we reduce, by degrading or excommunicating them, to the humbler place of penitents. And where for the sake of the church's peace and tranquillity we are not allowed to do this, we still do not reject the church's discipline; rather, we tolerate what we do not want so as to reach what we do want, observing the caution of the Lord's command, lest in wishing to gather the tares before the time we root up the wheat along with them. We also follow the example and precept of blessed Cyprian, who for the sake of peace bore with colleagues who were usurers, frauds and robbers, and did not become like them through contagion from them. Hence we too, if we are wheat, say with the fullest confidence the words of that same blessed martyr: that even if there seem to be tares in the church, neither our faith nor our love ought to be hindered so that, because we see tares in the church, we ourselves withdraw from the church. Our forebears would have spoken these words most justly and devoutly even if they had seen that Caecilian and some of his fellow bishops were wicked, since they still could not have separated them from the church because of those to whom their wickedness could not be demonstrated and who thought them good and innocent. These words they would certainly have spoken, this they would certainly have held, lest in rashly wishing to separate the tares they should root up the wheat as well.

As for the fact that a certain prophet was ordered neither to eat bread nor to drink water in Samaria, where he had been sent to rebuke those who had set up calves to be worshiped after the manner of the idols of Egypt: he was certainly bound to do what the Lord had commanded, for it pleased the Lord at that time to rebuke them in this way, that the prophet he had sent should touch no food there. Indeed this happens daily in the church: with those whom we rebuke more sharply we touch no food, even when we are on their property, so that they may feel how much we grieve over their sins. But must the people therefore be split apart as well, so that the weak, who cannot judge men's hearts or deeds unknown to them, even if those deeds are known to us, are indiscriminately uprooted like tender grass? For in that same Samaria were both Elijah and Elisha. They were in the wilderness, it is true, yet not because they were withdrawing over the sacraments, but because they were suffering persecution from wicked kings. And there, certainly not in some separate wilderness, were the seven thousand men, unknown even to Elijah, who had not bowed the knee before Baal. Finally, Samuel, held holy among the foremost, both rebuked Saul severely and yet went with him without demur to offer sacrifice to the Lord, and he was not defiled by contagion from Saul's sins but remained entirely clean by keeping his own merits.

But although this question has been plainly resolved both at the conference and now, let Haggai resolve it for us more plainly still, since they read out his testimony above the others, so that they now boast of it alone in place of all the rest. Through the prophet Haggai the Lord rebukes the people who had returned from Babylon, where they had been held captive, because they were neglecting the house of the Lord while adorning their own houses, and he says that for this reason he has struck their land with the plague of barrenness. Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and all that people, inspired by God, began to work on the house of the Lord their God. For the same scripture says: "And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of the remnant of all the people, and they came in and did work on the house of the Lord almighty, their God, on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius." See, even the day is specified on which they went in to work on the house of God. I take it that those men and that people working on the house of God were not unclean, especially since the Lord had said to them, "I am with you," and had stirred up their spirit to work well on his house. Then see what follows. For the same scripture continues: "In the seventh month, on the twenty-first day of the month, the Lord spoke by the hand of the prophet Haggai, saying to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to all the remnant of the people: Who is there among you who saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now, as though it were nothing in your sight? And now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, high priest; and be strong, all you people of the land, says the Lord almighty; and my Spirit rules in your midst. Take heart, for thus says the Almighty: Once more I will shake the heaven and the earth, the sea and the dry land, and I will shake all the nations, and the choice things of all the nations shall come, and I will fill this house, says the Lord almighty," and the rest that he adds, prophesying things to come. These are more correctly understood as referring to the times of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose people is the truest and holiest temple of God: not including those who are tolerated while mixed in among it, but consisting only of those who are now, for the present, spiritually separated from such people by living well, and who are later to be separated from them bodily as well. Nevertheless, how that people to whom this prophecy was foretold, and who were then working on the house of God, among whom were those two, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jehozadak, were encouraged and commended by the Lord is plain enough to see in these words of the prophet, which we have quoted exactly as they were spoken. Can we then call this people unclean, so that anyone who approaches it will be defiled, this people to whom it is said: "And now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, high priest; and be strong, all you people of the land, says the Lord almighty; and my Spirit rules in your midst"? Who but a complete madman would say that this is a people which defiles anyone who approaches it?

Now then, notice what Scripture goes on to add after the prophecy given to this people about the times of Christ: "On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year under King Darius, the word of the Lord came to Haggai the prophet, saying: Thus says the Almighty: Ask the priests about the law, saying: If a man carries consecrated meat in the fold of his garment, and the fold of his garment touches bread or stew or wine or any food, will it become holy? And the priests answered and said: No. And Haggai said: If someone defiled in soul touches any of these, will it become defiled? And the priests answered and said: It will be defiled. And Haggai answered and said: So is this people and so is this nation in my sight, says the Lord, and so are the works of their hands. And whoever goes near it will be defiled, because of their early-morning presumptions before the face of their labours; and you hated those who rebuked in the gates." Who is this people, so unclean that whoever goes near it is defiled? Is it the people to whom it was said, "Be strong, and my Spirit is in your midst"? Far from it! So there were two: one unclean, and the other forbidden to go near the unclean, the one urged to be strong because the Spirit of God was in their midst. If, then, there were two, let them show us two temples too, one that this people entered and another that the other entered; let them show us two altars, one on which this people offered sacrifices and another on which the other did; let them show us priests as well, some belonging to this people and others to that, each group sacrificing separately for its own people. But if anyone who tries to claim this is out of his mind, then these two peoples were within one people, under one high priest, entering one temple, just as under the one Moses there were some who offended God and some who pleased God. Of these the apostle says: "Not with all of them was God well pleased." He does not say, "With all of them God was not well pleased," as though all of them had displeased God; he says, "Not with all of them was God well pleased"—so with some, though not with all. And all of them were under the same priests, in one and the same tabernacle, and offered their victims on one and the same altar; and yet they were distinguished from one another by their deeds, not by place; by their hearts, not by the temple; by their conduct, not by altars. In this way some did not go near others so as not to be defiled by them; that is, they did not consent to their evil deeds, so as not to be condemned along with them. For Moses, so great a prophet, was not unaware even of those wicked men, whose impious murmurings and dreadful bitterness he endured every day. But let us suppose that he did not know them: did Samuel not know Saul either, whom God had condemned by an eternal sentence spoken through Samuel's own mouth? And yet he saw both Saul and holy David entering the one tabernacle of God and taking part in the same sacrifices. But he certainly saw them as distinct, because he saw them as distinct persons: the one he loved forever, the other he bore with for a time. So too Haggai knew that within one people there were two peoples entering one temple and living under one high priest. One he declared unclean, the other he forbade to go near the unclean; and yet he did not separate either them or himself from that same temple and those same altars. What he forbade, then, was a spiritual approach, consent to their deeds. The words themselves cry this out, if there are ears not shut by raging animosity or blocked by the din of empty quarrelling. For the prophet says: "Whoever goes near it will be defiled." He marked out the vice that must not be approached; he did not shut people off from people by physical separation. And one approaches the vice of corruption through the vice of consent.

Someone might say that the people to whom it was first said, "Be strong, for my Spirit is in your midst," had changed for the worse within a few days, so that it deserved to hear, "So is this people and so is this nation; whoever goes near it will be defiled"—for about ninety days are counted between the words spoken in that people's favour and these words commanding that its uncleanness be avoided. So that no one may think that this good people had become so very bad in so short a space of time, see what follows; notice what is said on that very day, the twenty-fourth of the ninth month, the day on which it was said, "So is this people and so is this nation; whoever goes near it will be defiled." For when he had said this and recounted their evil deeds, for which they were shown to be unclean, adding also, "You hated those who rebuked in the gates," he immediately went on: "And now set it in your hearts from this day and before, before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord: you who, when you put twenty measures of barley into the bin, found they became ten, and when you went into the winepress to draw off fifty jars, found they became twenty. I struck you with barrenness, and all the works of your hands with blight and hail, and you did not turn to me, says the Lord. Set your hearts, therefore, from this day onward, from the twenty-fourth of the ninth month; and from the day on which the temple of the Lord was founded, set it in your hearts, whether anything will yet be found on the threshing floor, or whether the vine or the apple tree or the fig and the pomegranate and the olive trees, which have not borne fruit. From this day I will bless." See: on that very day they were found worthy even of blessing. I think, then, that this blessing does not belong to those whose uncleanness he forbids anyone to approach, but to the good, who are forbidden to approach it. So in one people they were both mingled and separated: mingled by bodily contact, separated by the withdrawal of the will. But Scripture speaks in its usual way: it rebukes the wicked as though all in that people were wicked, and comforts the good as though all there were good. So your bishops, even in what they are said to have written after they were defeated at the conference, cited the prophecy of Haggai in our favour, and thereby reminded us how to prove more clearly what we say: that in one people, in one temple, under the same priests, amid the same sacraments, where people live with unlike wills and are at odds in their different ways of life, neither does one case prejudice another case nor one person another person.

There is also the passage from the apostle's letter which they now cite in their writings, where he says, "Do not be yoked together with unbelievers; for what fellowship has light with darkness?" and the rest, which we quoted above, showing how it ought rightly to be understood. What else do they achieve by citing it but to remind us to whom the apostle wrote these words? For in that very same people of the Corinthians we can demonstrate what we are saying, so that they may not suppose it was only the custom of the prophets, belonging to the usage of the Old Testament rather than the New, to rebuke the blameworthy as though everyone in that people were being rebuked, and to address the praiseworthy as though everyone there were being praised. See how the apostle speaks to the Corinthians: "Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, to the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, together with all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, theirs and ours: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that has been given you in Christ Jesus, that in everything you have been made rich in him, in all speech and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed among you, so that you lack nothing in any gift." Who, hearing this, would believe that there were any reprobates in the church of the Corinthians, since these words sound as though this praise were addressed to all? And yet a little later he says: "I beseech you, brothers, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you." And again, as though rebuking and reproaching them all for this dreadful vice, he says: "Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?" Now I think that those in that people who said, "I belong to Christ," were not yoked together with those who said, "I belong to Paul," "I to Apollos," "I to Cephas"; and yet they all came to one altar, and those who did not share the same vices shared the same sacraments. For it was to these same Corinthians that this too was said: "Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself." What else was the apostle thinking of but these empty talkers, so that it was not enough for him to say, "eats and drinks judgment," without adding "on himself," lest this should apply also to those who ate alongside them, yet did not eat judgment?

Among these same Corinthians there were also some who did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, which is the distinctive faith of Christians. That is why the apostle says to them: "Now if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?" He did not say "in this land" or "in this world"; he said "among you." Nor could he have used the resurrection of Christ as a settled premise except with people who were already Christians, to whom he says of that very resurrection of Christ: "So we preach, and so you believed." Now let us consider the words with which he praises the church of the Corinthians at the beginning of the letter, saying: "I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that has been given you in Christ Jesus, that in everything you have been made rich in him, in all speech and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed among you, so that you lack nothing in any gift." See: they had been so enriched in Christ in all speech and all knowledge, they so lacked nothing in any gift, that there were among them people who even then did not believe in the resurrection of the dead. Yet I think that those who lacked nothing in any gift were not yoked together with those who did not believe that the dead would rise. See how the faithful are not yoked together with unbelievers, even though they are mingled in the same people and are initiated in the same sacraments under the same priests.

Indeed, so that those whose faith already held to the resurrection of the dead should not consent to this unbelief, the apostle himself did not command them to separate physically. For there were many of them, unlike the single man who had his father's wife, whom he judges to deserve a more outspoken rebuke and excommunication. That man must be dealt with in one way, and a multitude infected with vice must be cared for and healed in quite another, lest, if people were separated from people, the wheat too should be rooted up through the crime of schism. So the apostle does not physically separate those who already believed in the resurrection of the dead from those in the same people who did not believe in it; yet he does not cease to separate them spiritually, saying: "Do not be led astray; bad conversations corrupt good morals." What he fears is not their meeting but their consent, lest they put faith in the bad conversations that corrupt good morals. So he warns them to be separated in conduct, not at the altar. Finally, before the apostle wrote this to them, there were in the same church people who did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, and in it too were those who lacked nothing in any gift; and the former did not defile the latter by their unbelief, because the latter did not consent to them in that unbelief. See how one does not go near it, lest whoever goes near be defiled; see how light has no fellowship with darkness; see how, although both kinds of fish swim within the same nets, neither does one case prejudice another nor one person another person.

Since this is so, what folly is so crude, what sleep of the heart so iron-hard, that it would not be shaken off and at last come to see that the case of Caecilian cannot prejudice the catholic world, with which the party of Donatus is not in communion, if the case of Maximian does not prejudice the party of Donatus—or rather the case of Felician and Primian, now joined together, who a little before had condemned each other? It is surely enough, to speak on their own terms, that bad fish hiding beneath the waves do not pollute the fishermen who do not know of them—though the question is not about the fishermen, whom the Lord perhaps meant to be understood as angels in that parable. What deserves more attention is that within the nets themselves the good fish cannot be stained by the bad. For they do see one another as they swim together, though they are not seen by the fishermen while they are under the water. But, as I said, it is enough for our case that the wicked do not pollute others when their evil deeds are not known.

There were in Caecilian's time certain blessed peacemakers who, even if he had not been innocent and they knew it, would have borne with him for the sake of catholic unity. Seeing him bound in the fellowship of the sacraments with so many unknown nations, through which that unity is spread abroad, and seeing that he could not be shown to them to be the kind of man they themselves knew him to be, they would have defended themselves against these slanders in the words of the blessed and peaceable Cyprian, and cried out confidently, saying: "We do not abandon unity on account of Caecilian, because, even if there seem to be tares in the church, neither our faith nor our charity ought to be hindered, so that because we see tares in the church we ourselves should withdraw from the church." To the peaceable patience of such men would belong that most glorious praise with which the angel of the church at Ephesus is praised—an angel whom no one of right understanding doubts to represent that church itself—to whom the Spirit says in the Apocalypse: "I know your works and your labour and your patience, and that you cannot bear evil people, and you have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and have found them liars; and you have patience, and have borne them for my name's sake, and have not grown weary." So let those be praised who lived this life in Caecilian's time, who for the sake of the Lord's name—which like ointment poured out was already fragrant through countless nations over the whole world—did not grow weary, bearing most patiently even one whom they knew to be wicked, if he was wicked, since he could not, on their judgment alone, be shown to others to be such and be torn away and separated from them. Our case is different; we ought not to claim for ourselves the praise of this patience. For we cannot say that we tolerated for the sake of peace something that could never come to our knowledge at all. For us the case of Caecilian lay beneath the waves. Our voice is the same as that of all the other Christian nations, against whom these men have found nothing whatever to say. Yet we rightly believe that Caecilian's case, unknown to us, is a good one, since we read that he was condemned once by a faction of his enemies, but acquitted three times when they themselves were the accusers. Otherwise let them believe the nearly one hundred bishops of the party of Donatus about the crimes of Primian, and then let them compel us to believe their seventy forebears about the crimes of Caecilian. And as for their saying that Caecilian, by his silence, confirmed the crimes charged against him at that council when he was absent, then Primian too confirmed the crimes charged against him by a hundred bishops, since it is not shown that he cleared himself of them even afterwards.
