But evidently one case does not prejudice another, nor one person another, when that would diminish the party of Donatus; yet it does prejudice, when that would divide the inheritance of Christ! Or does the case of Caecilian not prejudice the catholic unity that we hold and in whose fellowship we rejoice, though Caecilian was bishop of Carthage, while the case of Novellus of Tizica and Faustinus of Thuburbo prejudices it? These are men whom they did not even think worth accusing afterwards, as they did Caecilian and Felix; men whose names—indeed, the very names of the towns where they were—are not known to the whole of Africa, perhaps not even to the whole proconsular province. See: these are the little fish, lurking so deep down, even if they were bad, whose case they want to prejudice the case of so great a catch, whose full nets are spread over the whole world—little fish who could scarcely have been known even to the fish swimming beside them. And why should we not believe that these men too were innocent, since, as I said, they were not even thought worth accusing by them afterwards, and that man could be cleared whom their forebears, in the hostile conspiracy of that council, called the source of all evils?

But whatever these men were, what has it to do with us? They do not really deny us the point that the case and person of these unknown men does not prejudice the case and person of the catholic church, if one case does not prejudice another nor one person another. And yet, to go on leading you astray, they accuse us of having given gold to the judge so that he would pronounce sentence for us and against them. Tell us, if you can, how much we would have had to give your bishops, chosen as advocates, to get them to say or produce so much against themselves and for us, so that they argued our case and destroyed their own. What price would we have had to pay so that, after Primian's words, "It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of traditors should come together," they should nevertheless come and meet together with us, which they had said was unworthy? What price would we have had to pay so that, in the manner of advocates in the courts, they should try to raise technical objections against us about dates and days and even about persons, and so show plainly enough to everyone, even those unable to follow our arguments, how bad a case they had, since they were so afraid to set it out and argue it before a judge whose kindness and justice towards them they had praised so loudly, and whom they had so far not found ill-disposed towards them in any way? What price would we have had to pay so that they themselves should then demand that the matter be dealt with not by the formulas of the courts but rather by the testimonies of God, and promise that they too would answer from the holy Scriptures; and then, when the mandate of the catholic council that we had submitted was read out, and it became clear, even by their own admission, that we had wanted to argue the case of the catholic church from the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, they should go back again, as if they had forgotten what they had said they wanted, to those same courtroom objections, with tangled and odious wrangling?

What price would we have had to pay so that, disturbed by the number of our signatures shown in that same mandate, they should demand the presence of our whole council—a council from which only eighteen of us were present, in accordance with the edict of the judge—and should raise a charge of forgery, on the grounds that some could have been put up to sign in place of others? For it came to this: their numbers too were checked, and they themselves were caught in the very forgery of which they had tried to cast suspicion on us. Not only were some found in their mandate to have signed on behalf of absent men who had not even come to Carthage, but one man was called whose name was read and who did not answer. They said he had died on the road; and when they were asked how a man who had already died on the road could have signed at Carthage, after great difficulty, confusion and inconsistent, shifting answers, they asserted that he had died on the road not on his way there, but while returning home after he had signed. Then, questioned under solemn oath before God whether it was certain that he had been at Carthage, they were thrown into still greater confusion and said: "What if someone else stood in for him?" And so by their own words they confirmed that the forgery they had charged us with had appeared in their own mandate and had been clearly proven.

What price would we have had to pay so that, when they wanted to boast of their numbers, they should betray their lies in this too? For when a somewhat larger number of ours had attended, and we had said that about a hundred other catholic bishops had not come to Carthage, kept away partly by old age, partly by ill health, partly by various necessities, on hearing this they said that many more of theirs had not come. So too now, boasting that there are more than four hundred of them throughout Africa, they have forgotten what they put in their official notice: that they had all come to Carthage, so much so that, apart only from those whom bodily illness had detained either in their own sees or on the road, neither great age nor the toil of a long journey could keep away even the most aged of them. And the signatures read out in their mandate numbered, as the court staff reported after making the count, two hundred and seventy-nine, including those found to be forged and those who had signed on behalf of absent men, on the grounds that they had been detained by illness and could not come to Carthage. How then can it be true that they number more than four hundred, when they said that the only ones who had not come to Carthage were those kept away by bodily illness, and when others signed even on behalf of some of these—not to say that this was done for all who were ill? Or perhaps a plague had fallen on them, suddenly striking down a third of them? Yet they had been summoned by their primate in a letter of summons to drop everything and hurry to assemble at Carthage, so that they should know that whoever refused to come would have cheated them of the best thing they had in their case. This, evidently, was the best thing in their case: that a huge number of them should be seen—as though something were found all the more easily the greater the crowd of blind men looking for it.

What price would we not have paid for this? With both sides agreeing, the hearing had been adjourned to the day after next, and on the day before it they asked in a written notice that the court staff issue our mandate to them so that they could come prepared. Their excuse was that the staff could not keep up with writing out the record in so short a time. And so, on the next day of the hearing, they were shown to be going against what they themselves had agreed, even though the adjournment they asked for and received was a just one, since they had considered the case, which was wholly contained in our mandate, and found themselves in great difficulty. What could be more just than for men thrown into confusion by such solid truth to ask for an adjournment? If only it had done them some good! If only, having considered our mandate, to which they could not reply at all, they had chosen to correct their perversity rather than make it worse! So they were right to ask for an adjournment. But on the day before, they ought not to have said in their notice that our mandate had to be issued to them so that they could come prepared on the appointed day because the stenographers could not keep up with writing out the record, and then, on the very day of the session, complain again about those same stenographers for not keeping up. What drove them to this but violent agitation, when they saw that in drawing up our mandate we had argued the case in such a way that they could find no reply? And what price would we not have paid for this too: that they asked for and received that very adjournment, six days long, so that no one could say they had been unable to answer our mandate for lack of time?

Then, on the third day of our conference itself, what price would we not have paid for this? By utterly empty and pointless delaying tactics they showed that they had no wish at all to come to the substance of the case, and their very fear proclaimed how bad a case they had. Their fear even burst out as testimony in the plainest words, when they said, 'We are gradually being drawn into the case,' and in another place, 'Your Excellency sees that we are gradually being led into the inner substance of the case.' O force of truth, stronger than any rack or iron claws for wringing out a confession! So many bishops gather from all over Africa. They enter Carthage with such a grand and splendid procession that they draw upon themselves the eyes and attention of that great city. Those who are to speak for all are chosen by all. A place worthy of so great an affair is found in the middle of the city. Both sides assemble, the judge is present, the records lie open, and everyone waits in suspense for the outcome of so great a conference. Then the most select and most eloquent men labor with all the strength that ought to have gone into doing something, so that nothing is done. They try to examine the standing of the parties in the manner of the law courts, a question over which litigants commonly wear away years on end. Yet in that very session they had acknowledged that the Catholics had drawn up their mandate with divine testimonies rather than with legal formulas, and had promised to reply from the scriptures in the same way. And God, by his wonderful help, willed that while they were inquiring who the plaintiff was so as to avoid coming to the case, that very inquiry into the plaintiff should suddenly bring the case out into the open. Then these distinguished men, who seemed to have been chosen to argue the case, cry out and testify instead that they had been chosen not to argue it. They complain resentfully to the judge that they are gradually being drawn into the inner substance of the case, as though anything else ought to have been dealt with, all else set aside, than the very thing they were unwilling to deal with so long after, or so late. For they never wanted it dealt with at all where they feared defeat. Who could have shaken so open an utterance of this fear out of their closed hearts? I do not say if we had enriched them with the most lavish gifts, but even if we had tortured them with the cruelest punishments!

They were inquiring into the standing of the plaintiffs with legal hair-splitting, and wanted to show that we were the plaintiffs, so that they would be allowed to examine our standing by legal right and find delays that would last for years. To this end they read a petition of ours, once given to the proconsul, in which we had asked that they be summoned so that the very conference between us which we have now obtained from the emperor might take place then, and by that petition they tried to show that we were in effect the plaintiffs. We replied that we had always wanted a conference to take place, not so as to bring charges against them, but so as to clear ourselves of the charges they habitually bring. For this is precisely why they are heretics and separated from the unity of the church: they bring charges which they cannot prove. Next, the commissioner seemed to be following the order of time, giving precedence to our petition, produced by them, over the records we had produced, in which they too had asked the prefects for a conference, because the petition came earlier in time than those prefectural records. Taking the opportunity the commissioner offered, we very easily and very justly obtained this: that if he was giving precedence to whatever was shown to be earlier in time, he should rather order the reading of the document in which they themselves, through the proconsul Anullinus, accused Caecilian before the emperor Constantine. These are the crimes of Caecilian that they charge against our communion, and that we wished to clear in that conference. So, once the reading began, since they were there most plainly defeated on every point, they began to shout, 'We are gradually being drawn into the case,' and again, 'Your Excellency sees that we are gradually being led into the inner substance of the case.' O great, but hardly surprising, confusion! When would a demon fear an exorcist as much as they feared the reading of those documents? For they made it plain that Caecilian had been accused before the emperor by their predecessors, and acquitted in so many trials, not only episcopal but imperial as well.

When, or at what price, could we have bought this? Thrown into confusion by that very fear, they even dared to fall back on their plea that the time had run out, in which they had said that the case had already lapsed and, since four months had passed, could no longer be heard at all. What does this mean? What more fitting witness to their state of mind could be found than this fear, so plainly expressed, so open? Fear usually takes away freedom, yet they were so free in their fear that they did not hide in silence their own verdict on their bad case but gave it away in the plainest words. O violent alarm, fit to wring out a confession! Fear sprang from their mouths with such force that before its onslaught shame fled from their faces. As long as the documents showing that Caecilian had been accused and cleared were not being read, they were searching for plaintiffs for the sake of arguing the case, and examining the standing of the parties. Snares of delay were evasively being woven so that the case itself would never be reached, yet even these demands seemed to be made, as if by right, for the sake of arguing the case. But once Caecilian's excellent case was brought forward to be read, the plea of time, already exploded and refuted, is brought back, and they cry out that the day for arguing the case has already passed.

Why are you still waiting to hear what the commissioner pronounced in our favor, when you see what your bishops' fear pronounced against themselves? The commissioner himself had certainly given them leave to appoint another judge of their choosing to sit with him. They refused, because if they had chosen someone, they could not have lied to you that he too had been bribed by us. But they did what they refused to do. They did indeed appoint another judge to sit with him, not some outsider but one most intimate with them. See: their own fear was the other judge. He certainly received nothing from us, and he judged freely in our favor. He showed no favor to the very men inside whom he dwelt. He came out of their secret chamber, and he judged first, before the case was argued, because he had come to know it first, in their own hearts. In short, the one came forward to learn the case, the other came forward already knowing it. The one judged by presiding, listening and speaking, the other simply by stepping out into the open. I think they were right after all to say that the case should no longer be argued, for how much more quickly the litigants' fear settled it than the commissioner's labor! The one was asking what was to be read from their papers; the other revealed what was going on in their hearts.

Terrified by the documents that had been brought forward to be read, they had come to the point of saying that the case had already lapsed through time and could not be heard. So they put to us a proposal on a matter already settled: if we argued from the holy scriptures, those documents should not be read at all, but if we chose to have them read, they had a valid plea that the time had run out, so that they would not allow the case to be argued at all, since it had lapsed through time. Yet they themselves had not kept their earlier promise. They had acknowledged that in our mandate we argued the church's case with the testimonies of the scriptures, and had promised to reply to it likewise with the testimonies of the scriptures. Instead they contended that the standing of the plaintiffs must be examined, not in the manner of disputants, but in the manner of litigants. We therefore replied that if they preferred to deal with nothing except the question which and where the Catholic Church is, we would argue her case only by the divine testimonies by which she was foretold. But if they brought charges against men, then since they themselves could not establish those charges by divine testimonies but only by documents of some other kind, we too would clear them by documents of that kind. So, while they kept repeating their empty arguments, we repeated this most persistently; and so truth overcame them and, refuted and defeated as they were, compelled them to hear what we had brought forward. For they saw that if they charged our communion with none of Caecilian's crimes, nothing would be left them by which they could in any way excuse their separation from unity. But if they did charge it with Caecilian's crimes, these could not be asserted by them except by such documents, nor defended by us in any other way.

Then again, amid all their quarrelsome din, what price would we not have paid for this? We said that our proposal was this: that they should prove, if they could, the crimes they habitually charge against our communion, which is spreading through all nations, so that it might be learned whether their separation had been just. They replied that we wanted to argue someone else's case, that is, the case of the churches overseas, against which they were bringing no such charges. This dispute, they said, was among Africans, and those churches ought rather to wait, so that they might join to themselves whichever side won in this conference, and then the winners would share the Catholic name with them. Why then do you still ask, why do you still hesitate, which church you ought to hold to? There you have her: the church against which your bishops admitted they have no case, to which our communion is joined and from which theirs is separated. For if they have now said that she ought to wait so that whoever defeats us may be joined to her and share the Catholic name with her, then surely our forebears defeated their forebears long ago. That is why they were joined to that church and held the Catholic name in her unity. And if these men have already been defeated by our forebears in the persons of their own forebears, why do they go on contending with us to this day? But if they have not been defeated, why are they not in communion with that church, which they cannot deny is Catholic and against which they admitted they have no case? Look at the Catholic Church overseas, spread among so many nations, which they said ought to wait so as to join the winners to herself. How can she wait to join the winners to herself unless she is untouched by the crimes that are in dispute between us? For if she is not untouched by them, she herself is guilty and defeated along with the defeated, so how will she join the victors to herself? But if, as they admit, she is untouched by these crimes, then we too are untouched, since we cleave to her in the same communion. For if that communion means another's crime defiles us, then our crime also defiles her with whom we are in communion. Yet they admitted that she is not polluted by the crime of the Africans, even though the Africans share with her in the communion of the sacraments. In that, therefore, they were proved wrong: we too could not have been polluted by the crime of those with whom we share in the communion of the sacraments, since we are entangled with them in no bond of consent. Indeed, these same words of theirs very easily show that Caecilian's own case was the winning one. For if, while we are in conflict, the overseas church, untouched by these crimes, must wait so as to join the winners to herself and to the Catholic name, then she was waiting when their forebears were fiercely contending with Caecilian. So he was the winner then, since after the conflict the church which had waited for its outcome joined him to herself. Or if she could both join him to herself in the communion of the sacraments though he was polluted and, as they have now admitted, remain unpolluted by these crimes, then all the more have we won. For this shows that each bears his own burden, and that no case prejudges another case and no person prejudges another person.

And then, what price would we not have paid for this: that they thought they should reply to our mandate, in which we had covered the whole case, not with impromptu speech but in writing? For this made it plain that they could not answer all the points set out in our mandate, which they would not even touch on in their document. Nor can anyone say that they could not keep our argument in their memory and so did not choose to answer all the essential points. Our mandate was issued to them at their request, made in a written notice, on the very ground that they could then come prepared to answer everything. And although seven men had already been chosen by the rest to do everything on behalf of all, they nevertheless produced the document in which they tried to answer our mandate in the name of their whole council, as if it were a letter from all of them to the commissioner. Had we refused to admit it, we would have been fully within our rights, for it was out of order, once the case had been entrusted to seven men, for anything to be done except through those who had been chosen. But so as not to seem to fear their document, set against our own, we agreed without any hesitation that it should be read and entered into the record. For it was something to be wished for, and, as I said, something worth paying for, that after the many days' adjournment we had granted at their request they should bring us the product of their midnight labor. Anyone reading both documents could then see plainly that they had not answered our mandate, and it would be evident that we had answered that very document of theirs at once, without any delay. For even if some people are so slow-witted as to think they said something in the places in our mandate where they chose not to remain silent, I do not think anyone is so stupid as to suppose that they gave any reply in the places where they were completely silent. And these are not small or negligible points. On the contrary, the whole case rests on them.

For the testimonies of the scriptures by which we showed that the church with which we are in communion began from Jerusalem and is spreading through the whole world they passed over as though they had never been cited at all, crushed by the great weight of divine authority. Likewise, what our mandate said about the blessed Cyprian, who taught by precept and confirmed by his own example that the wicked are to be tolerated within the church rather than the church being abandoned on their account, they did not dare to touch at all. I believe they understood that if they tried to undermine Cyprian's authority in any of his writings, they would be admitting that we too are right not to yield to his authority where they habitually cite his opinions or decrees on repeating baptism. And yet they would not openly mention even Cyprian's view on baptism, knowing that there too, if they did, they would suffer shipwreck. For Cyprian did not abandon unity, but remained in it together with those who thought differently on this matter. So either we must say that the church perished then, and that there no longer was any church from which their Donatus could be born, or else, as is true, the church survived, and within it the wicked do not defile the good, as Cyprian also judged, since he remained in the same universal church with those who thought differently. And so these men have taken on themselves the detestable sacrilege of schism, for they ought in no way to have separated themselves from the unity spread through the whole world because of the crimes of some people or other, crimes never proved and which would not have justified it even if they were true. As far as one can tell, they foresaw this, and so passed over in complete silence that testimony of Cyprian which our mandate mentioned.

Then there is what they themselves also declared by their own judgment in the case of the Maximianists: that unity must not be abandoned on account of the wicked. They said that Maximian's associates had not been polluted by Maximian, and they received back with their rank intact some of those they had condemned. And they showed that the baptism of Christ, even when given outside the church, is to be recognized rather than destroyed, since they did not dare to rebaptize those who had been baptized by Felician in schism and were afterwards received back together with him. When they read this too in our mandate, they decided that it was better to keep silent and pass it over than to reopen the wound by any rebuttal. Our mandate also distinguished the case of Caecilian from the case of the church, and yet defended Caecilian's case too on every side; in their reply they did not touch it at all. Who, then, could suppose that they answered that mandate of ours, when they did not attempt to say a single word against all these points, nor even to give the faintest shadow of any reply at all? As for what they appeared to answer, let anyone who wishes read their document, compare it with that same mandate of ours, and judge, not to mention the reply we gave at once, by which all the contrivances of their emptiness were overthrown.

Then again, even if we gave mountains of gold, when could we have bought this? The case of Maximian was put to them, so that they would understand that the council in which seventy bishops pronounced whatever they pleased against Caecilian in his absence did Caecilian no harm, just as it did Primian no harm when about a hundred bishops likewise condemned him in his absence on Maximian's behalf. Violently agitated and driven into dreadful straits, they replied that no case prejudges another case and no person prejudges another person. In these very few words they confirmed that our whole case, over which we had been contending with them earlier, was entirely unbeaten. For what else were we doing, when with so many testimonies from the holy scriptures and on such authority, that of prophets, apostles, bishops and our very opponents, we showed that the good are not polluted by the wicked through the communion of the sacraments if they differ in heart, will, conduct and deeds, and so have separate cases and are separate persons? What else were we laboring for, but to make it clear that no case prejudges another case and no person prejudges another person? This they said briefly, compelled by sheer necessity, because when we had been saying it at length they would not yield to the truth.

And with what treasures, what riches, what heaps of precious stones should we have bought this? They did not hesitate not only to admit, but even to proclaim and boast, that their forebears had prosecuted Caecilian before the emperor Constantine, and they even tried to assert, falsely, that he had been condemned by the emperor. Where now is that cry with which they have habitually deceived you, stirring up resentment against us for pleading the church's case before the emperor? Where are the words of Primian recorded in the proceedings before the magistrate of Carthage: 'They bring the rescripts of many emperors; we offer only the gospels'? Where is that splendid praise with which they extol their separation, saying that the church of truth is the one that suffers persecution, not the one that inflicts it? It has surely been shattered, surely laid low. Their speeches are read out, and they cannot deny them, because their signatures are read out too. We have them confessing, proclaiming and boasting that their forebears harshly persecuted Caecilian before the emperor. We also have them claiming that Caecilian was condemned by the emperor at their persecuting instance. Let them stop crying out, then, that their faction is the church of truth because it does not inflict persecution but suffers it, or else let them admit that it was not the church of truth when Caecilian was suffering at the hands of their forebears. For if those who suffer persecution are automatically good, Caecilian was good when he suffered it. But if it is possible for the wicked also to suffer persecution, while those who inflict it cannot be good, then their forebears were not good when they persecuted Caecilian. And if it is possible both for the good to inflict persecution and for the wicked to suffer it, then we are not to be blamed, nor are they to be praised, simply because they suffer something like what they boast Caecilian suffered at their forebears' hands. And yet it was not established at all that Caecilian had been condemned by the emperor. On the contrary, his acquittal and vindication had been established by the reading of the episcopal and imperial verdicts, and nothing could be proved to have overturned them afterwards. So it turned out that, once Caecilian's condemnation, about which they had lied, was set aside, what remained was the persecution which they admitted their forebears had carried out.

It was not enough for them to dare to boast falsely that Caecilian had been condemned by the emperor, and then to be unable to prove what they asserted. On top of that, they actually proved the opposite, and gave strong support to our own documents on the matter: that Caecilian's acquittal had remained perfectly firm, and had not, as they had falsely claimed, been reversed by a later judgment of the emperor. First they asked for Optatus, the Catholic bishop of the church of Milevis, to be read out, promising to prove from him that Caecilian had been condemned by the emperor. When the reading turned out rather to tell against them, no one could keep from laughing. That laughter could certainly not have gone into the written record of the proceedings, and would have passed quite unnoticed, had they not refused to let it pass unnoticed by saying: 'Let those who laughed listen.' This was indeed written down and signed. The passage they wanted read in their favour was ambiguous. So the judge, quite rightly, ordered the passage a little before it to be read, so that those words might become clear if possible. What was read was exactly what they did not want: that Caecilian had been cleared. The passage they had first offered showed him not condemned, as they boasted, but detained at Brescia for the sake of peace. When they then said that in those words Optatus had meant to play down Caecilian's condemnation, they were told to read out some clear condemnation of Caecilian from another source, so that it could be shown that Optatus had played it down. For Optatus had written quite plainly that Caecilian had been cleared. Since they could not do this at all, they put forward and used up every needless detour of delay, and then began quite openly to help us. It was as if they had been briefed by us, or chosen along with us to defend and proclaim Caecilian's innocence. They were asked to show, if they could, what they were claiming: that Caecilian had been condemned by the emperor in a later judgment. This was the same emperor whose letter we had read showing him acquitted. In reply they produced a petition that their predecessors had presented to that same emperor Constantine, which showed quite plainly that it was rather they who had been condemned by his judgment. What happened to them before the imperial power was what happened to the enemies of holy Daniel, who suffered from those same lions what they had wanted the innocent man to suffer. When we briefly pointed out that they had read out that petition for us and against themselves, they added something more. They produced a letter of the same emperor addressed to the vicar Verinus, in which he expressed strong disgust for them, left them to the judgment of the Lord, who had already begun to take vengeance on them, and released them from exile by a most humiliating act of indulgence. So it was established beyond all doubt not only that no condemnation of Caecilian had followed afterwards, but also that his acquittal and clearing had been confirmed both by their punishment and by that contemptuous indulgence. These excellent documents, it must be admitted, we did not have in hand. Perhaps, if we had heard that they existed somewhere where they would not be given to us free, we would have paid any price to be allowed to copy them. And how much would we have paid, had it been up for sale, to have them read out on our behalf by our adversaries themselves?

What more could possibly be added for them to help us still more? And yet they added it. They brought up the case of Felix of Abthugni, who had ordained Caecilian and against whom they had brought the charge of being a traditor, one who handed over the Scriptures. After Caecilian's acquittal, when pressure was being applied to achieve unity, they had raised the question of this Felix, thinking that in this way Caecilian, though already cleared, could be entangled in another man's crimes. So this case of Felix too was examined in the proconsul's court, where Felix's innocence came to light with perfect clarity. But in that same trial a certain Ingentius confessed that he had committed forgery against Felix. Since a bishop's case was involved, he could not easily be punished. Nor could the proconsul easily release a man accused of so great a crime without consulting the emperor, at whose urging all those proceedings were being carried out. So the proconsul referred the matter to him, and the emperor wrote back that Ingentius should be sent to his court. He wished the predecessors of these men, who were petitioning him daily, to be refuted in his presence. Yet he had no doubt at all about Felix's clearing; in fact he confirmed it [?] by the plain statement of his own words, as his rescript shows. We had all these documents of Felix's case in hand and had arranged to submit them to be read. But they forestalled us here, and were the first to produce and read the same emperor's letter about sending Ingentius to him. Perhaps we would not even have read these documents, since we thought it enough that Caecilian's own case had been settled in a way that seemed to require nothing more. But our adversaries were acting so that the persecution their predecessors had carried out against ours before the emperors, and their slanders, might appear all the more fully defeated. What were we to do but gladly accept what was offered and give thanks to the Lord in all things? So it was they themselves who produced Constantine's letter, and they themselves who read it. What I say seems incredible, but the proceedings bear witness: their statements were written down, and their signatures are on record. They themselves, I say, read out what Constantine had written: that Aelianus the proconsul had given Felix's case a proper hearing, and that Felix had been shown to be innocent of the crime of handing over the Scriptures. Constantine said he wanted Ingentius sent to his court only for this reason: 'so that,' he says, 'it may be made plain and declared to those who are pressing the case at present and do not cease to petition me day after day, while they are present and standing before me, that they have stirred up ill will against Caecilian in vain and have wished to rise up violently against him for nothing.' They read this themselves. Which of us would have dared to hope that truth would make our defenders of the very men whom iniquity had made our accusers? So too in ancient times Balaam, whom iniquity had hired to curse the people of God, was compelled by truth to bless them.

There was not enough time then to check the sequence of consuls. The books called consular lists were not at hand, and no one would have believed that they would raise so empty a point as to demand that we answer what was done after Ingentius was sent, or whether he was sent at all. After all, the proconsul's sentence had declared Felix innocent, and the emperor's reply, which they themselves produced and read, had confirmed that sentence. And they would certainly have produced the evidence themselves if they had been confident that anything was done in their favour after Ingentius was sent. But the sequence of consuls makes the order clear. First, Caecilian was acquitted by the episcopal judgment of Miltiades. Not long afterwards, Felix was found innocent in the proconsul's court. After that, Caecilian was also cleared by the emperor, who heard the case between the parties. Then, some years later, his adversaries were released by that humiliating indulgence. Miltiades gave judgment on 2 October, when Constantine was consul for the third time and Licinius for the second. Aelianus the proconsul heard Felix's case on 15 February, when Volusianus and Annianus were consuls, that is, about four months later. Constantine wrote to the vicar Eumalius about Caecilian's clearing on 10 November, when Sabinus and Rufinus were consuls, that is, two years and nearly eight months later. And the same emperor sent a letter to the vicar Valerius, ending their exile and leaving their fury to the vengeance of God, on 5 May, when Crispus and Constantine were consuls for the second time, that is, about four years and six months later. So it is established with perfect clarity and without any evasion that, whether or not Ingentius was sent to court, no judgment was afterwards given against Caecilian. On the contrary, imperial judgments as well afterwards declared him the victor over his adversaries and persecutors.

So let the party of Donatus go on now, so often disproved, slanderous, lying and refuted, so often defeated and confounded in every way. Let it go on boasting that we bribed the judge. As if the defeated ever said anything else! Of course the judge had to be bribed, so that his authority might undo what they themselves had done so well! Yet I would not say they acted badly. In fact they acted excellently, since they said so much for the truth against their own errors. If you consider their cause, the judge truly ruled against them; but if you read their statements, his ruling rather agreed with them. Or would the man in the middle have opposed us in a case where those on the opposing side spoke, produced and read so much in our favour? Why would we have needed to buy anything from the judge? We did not buy from our adversaries the things that would have forced the judge to rule for us even if he had taken money from them. And yet, if we did not know him to be a God-fearing man, a lover of justice and a stranger to all such sordid dealings, it is we who ought to have suspected him. Seeing them hard pressed by the truth, and not wishing to seem against them, he was far too patient with men who wandered through empty talk, said so many needless things and returned again and again to points already refuted. As a result the record is weighed down with so many volumes that nearly everyone is reluctant to unroll it and learn by reading how the case was conducted. Whether they did this more from lack of truth or by cunning design, I do not know. Yet this was the only way they could help in any way so wretched a cause, which they ought rather to have abandoned. Indeed, suppose the rest of their party were to accuse those who argued the case, and claim instead that we had bribed them to help our cause and destroy their own by all the statements they made and the readings they produced. I do not know how they could defend themselves and clear themselves of that suspicion, unless perhaps they said: 'If we had been bribed, we would also have quickly finished off so bad a cause, convicted both by us and by them. As it is, believe that we stood by you sincerely and wanted to be of some use, at least from this: by talking a great deal we made sure that the proceedings could not easily be read, and that our defeat would not quickly be recognized.' Had they not done this, perhaps no one would believe, even if both they and we swore to it, that they gave us free of charge all the many things they said and read for us against themselves. Yet for this we thank not them but God. For it was truth that forced them to bring forward and make public all those things for our cause, by speaking or by reading. Love did not draw them to it.

Therefore, brothers — if you are not angry that we call you brothers. For when they heard this from us, they declared in the record that they were being insulted. Even though they were reminded by our mandate, where this testimony from the prophet is set down, they could not recall that God commanded: 'Say, "You are our brothers," to those who hate you and detest you, so that the name of the Lord may be honoured and may appear to them in joy, but let them be put to shame.' So now, brothers, let the name of the Lord appear to you in joy. That name is invoked over us both, and we both bear its sacraments, so it is not without reason that we are called brothers. Love peace now. Now at least abandon this quarrelsome and slanderous habit, convicted and confounded as it is. And do not hate your bishops when they come over to us corrected; hate them rather when they persist in wicked error and still lead you astray. Nor should they think themselves great because we grant them in unity an honour which they may keep once they have been set free. For as long as they hold it outside unity, it makes them all the more deserving of condemnation. Military standards in the hands of usurpers do more harm than if they were not held at all. Yet when those men are corrected and brought back into the emperor's camp, the standards are not broken or done away with. Instead they begin to adorn and protect the very men whom they once betrayed and brought to punishment. Why do you still listen to their mad complaints and empty lies? The case was concluded at night, but so that the night of error might end. Sentence was pronounced at night, but it shone with the light of truth. They complained that they were shut in as if in a prison. We were there too: either both sides were wronged or both were treated with care. But how can we call it a wrong, when we remember that we were in so spacious, bright and cool a place? And how could it be a prison where the judge was too? Finally, we did not know we were locked in, though we were inside with them. How do they know, unless perhaps because they wanted to run away? But anyone can see that they would not be saying such empty things about so fine a judge, things more fit to be laughed at than refuted, if they could find anything solid to say for their cause. We know how many of you, perhaps all or nearly all, are used to saying: 'Oh, if only they would meet in one place! If only they would confer at last, so that the truth might appear from their debate!' Look, it has happened. Look, falsehood has been convicted. Look, truth has appeared. Why is unity still shunned? Why is love still despised? What need is there for us to be divided by the names of men? One God created us, one Christ redeemed us, and one Spirit ought to bind us together. Now let the name of the Lord be honoured and appear to you in joy, so that you may recognize your brothers in his unity. In the statements of your bishops the error that separated us has now been defeated. Let the devil at last be defeated in your hearts as well, and may Christ, who commanded this, be gracious to his flock, now gathered together and at peace.
(PAO 178, ed. Knöll.) After the Conference, Against the Donatists: One Book.

After the conference we held with their bishops, I also wrote a book addressed to the Donatists themselves. It is fairly long, I think, and I wrote it with care, so that they would not be led astray by their bishops any longer. Besides what I said there about the proceedings of the conference, so that what had taken place could be learned in brief, I also answered some of their empty claims that had reached us, which they put about after their defeat wherever and however they could. I did the same thing much more briefly in a further letter to them. But because everyone present at the council of Numidia agreed that this should be done, that letter is not counted among my own letters. It begins: "The aged Silvanus, Valentinus, Innocent, Maximinus, Optatus, Augustine, Donatus and the other bishops of the council of Zerta, to the Donatists."
This book begins: "Why, Donatists, do you still let yourselves be led astray?"
